ra_gate_reread.caveat: A 15% audit of the bucket, limited by what Crossref holds. It can show the rule failing; it cannot clear the 140 records that stayed invisible.

records.title: The Family Environment and Leaving the Parental Home
records.venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family
records.note: Family structure of origin against the timing of home-leaving, Canadian Family History Survey. Link 1 with a driver, no births.

records.title: Two Kinds of Preindustrial Household Formation System
records.note: Hajnal's simple-versus-joint household formation systems. The canonical statement of the pre-modern niche rule; A.7's under Ruling 2, carried here as theory.

records.title: Single Mothers and Poverty in Japan: The Role of Intergenerational Coresidence
records.note: Intergenerational co-residence as income sharing that mitigates single mothers' poverty in Japan, 67,252 observations. Arrangement as exposure, poverty as outcome.

records.title: Fertility cost, grandparental childcare, and female employment
records.note: No abstract; published version of 'Fertility cost, grandparental childcare, and female employment'.

records.title: Recent trends in fertility and household formation in the industrialized world.
records.note: Recent trends in fertility AND household formation in the industrialised world, analysed through postponement and recuperation. Puts the two links side by side at the aggregate level; the tempo framing matters for §9's TEMPO_OR_QUANTUM.

records.title: Fertility, Economy, and Household Formation in England over Three Centuries
records.note: Household formation rules and fertility in pre-transition England over three centuries. Exactly the pre-modern niche mechanism, which Ruling 2 leaves with A.7; carried here as theory and cross-reference.

records.title: How far do children move? Spatial distances after leaving the parental home
records.note: No abstract; 'How far do children move? Spatial distances after leaving the parental home' is the link between home-leaving and the PROXIMITY cell -- the record that would say whether leaving home and living near parents are the same treatment.

records.title: Patterns of low and lowest-low fertility in Europe
records.note: PUBLISHED VERSION of the Billari and Kohler lowest-low fertility analysis screened in batch 7 as W1541364795 (working paper). Cross-country correlations between total fertility and LEAVING THE PARENTAL HOME, marriage and female labour force participation. Duplicate pair -- keep this one at assembly; do not pool both.

records.title: Parenthood and Happiness: a Review of Folk Theories Versus Empirical Evidence
records.note: No abstract; parenthood and happiness review.

records.title: Cultural Dynamics and Economic Theories of Fertility Change
records.note: Lesthaeghe's ideational-change model of Western family formation. D.1.a's.

records.title: Leaving Home in Europe: The Experience of Cohorts Born Around 1960
records.note: Leaving home across 16 European countries from FFS data, focusing on the TIMING, SEQUENCING and SYNCHRONISATION of leaving home with union formation. A gated anchor; the synchronisation measure is the closest published handle on §3's joint determination.

records.title: Grandparental childcare and second births in China
records.note: Whether GRANDPARENTAL CHILDCARE raises the likelihood and speed of transition to SECOND BIRTH in China. C.2.a's exposure with a parity-specific fertility outcome; at least the fourth near-identical China second-birth childcare record in this frame, which is itself worth reporting.

records.title: Moving out the parental home and partnership formation as social determinants of low fertility
records.note: Gated anchor, in its Vienna Yearbook debate form: 'MOVING OUT THE PARENTAL HOME AND PARTNERSHIP FORMATION AS SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF LOW FERTILITY'. The registered hypothesis stated as a position in a field debate; the other contributions to the same debate are separate records in this batch and route out.

records.title: Patrilocality and Early Marital Co-residence in Rural China, 1955–85
records.note: Patrilocality and early marital co-residence in rural China 1955-85, testing modernisation against tradition-restored and demographic-determinism accounts. Exposure trend for the extended arm's largest setting, no fertility outcome.

records.title: Pathways to Childlessness
records.note: Pathways to childlessness from NSFH and a Dutch living-arrangements survey. Childlessness is the outcome but the arrangement is not the exposure; the NESTOR instrument may still be useful.

records.title: Leaving the Parental Home: Patterns in Six Latin American Countries
records.venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family
records.note: Sociodemographic determinants of leaving the parental household in six Latin American countries, World Fertility Survey. Exposure-trend baseline, no fertility outcome.

records.title: Disruptive decisions to leave home: Gender and family differences in expatriation choices
records.venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
records.note: No abstract; 'leaving home' here is expatriation for work.

records.title: Do grandparents really matter? The effect of regular grandparental childcare on the second-birth transition
records.note: Published ESR version of the reclassified anchor: regular GRANDPARENTAL CHILDCARE and the second-birth transition, framed through the work-family incompatibility that leaves fertility desires unrealised. C.2.a's.

records.title: Grandparenting and Childbearing in the Extended Family
records.venue: European Journal of Population / Revue européenne de Démographie
records.note: No abstract in this record, but this is the gated anchor 'Grandparenting and Childbearing in the Extended Family'. Primary-cell record; the design is not visible from the title alone.

records.title: The Timing of Leaving the Parental Home and Its Linkages to Other Life Course Events in Turkey
records.note: Turkish DHS: timing of leaving the parental home against labour force entry, family formation AND FIRST BIRTH, split into early, on-time and late home-leavers. Arrangement timing as exposure with a birth outcome. NOTE: same title as the Marriage & Family Review record already gated as an anchor -- likely a duplicate pair to resolve at assembly.

records.title: Parenthood and Leaving Home in Young Adulthood
records.note: No abstract, but 'Parenthood and Leaving Home in Young Adulthood' in Population Research and Policy Review names both links and the pre-launch population. Direction of the arrow is not visible from the title and matters -- trace.

records.title: Gender, Turning Points, and Boomerangs: Returning Home in Young Adulthood in Great Britain
records.note: Gated anchor. Rates of and factors behind RETURNING to the parental home in Great Britain, against the popular boomerang narrative. Link 1's return half, which §9's ARRANGEMENT_MEASURE has to accommodate.

records.title: The boomerang age: transitions to adulthood in families
records.note: 'The Boomerang Age' on less permanent living arrangements among young adults in Western societies. Book review; states the exposure trend.

records.title: Normal Stresses during the Transition to Parenthood
records.note: No abstract and the title — normal stresses during the transition to parenthood — is not decisive either way.

records.title: The Mental Health of Married, Cohabiting, and Non–Coresident Parents With Infants
records.note: Mental health of married, cohabiting and non-coresident parents; co-residence with a PARTNER.

records.title: Household Formation in Developed Societies
records.note: Household formation in developed societies as a demand-supply problem, with nine hypotheses for the trend toward separate living. The theory statement for link 1.

records.title: Employment Insecurity at Labour Market Entry and Its Impact on Parental Home Leaving and Family Formation
records.note: EMPLOYMENT INSECURITY at labour market entry against parental home leaving AND family formation, European graduate survey. Both links estimated on one cohort with a plausibly pre-determined exposure; C.5.a owns the treatment, but this is the structure §3 asks for. Priority read.

records.title: Leaving Home, Attending College, Partnership and Parenthood: The Role of Life Transition Events in Leisure Pattern Stability From Adolescence to Young Adulthood
records.note: No abstract; leaving home, college, partnership and parenthood as predictors of LEISURE pattern stability. The outcome is leisure.

records.title: Children Living with Parents Who Have a Substance Use Disorder
records.note: Children living with parents who have a substance use disorder.

records.title: Grandparental childcare, maternal labor force participation, and the birth of a second child: Further knowledge from empirical analysis
records.note: No abstract; grandparental childcare, maternal labour force participation and second birth. C.2.a's, and the labour-supply co-outcome again.

records.title: Family Values and Coresidence with Married Children in Urban China
records.note: Co-residence of parents with MARRIED children in urban China, and the finding that it persists despite non-traditional values -- so it is not simply a norms story. Bears on Wall 3; the arrangement is the outcome.

records.title: Europe's demographic issues: fertility, household formation and replacement migration
records.note: No abstract; 'Europe's demographic issues: fertility, household formation and replacement migration' names both links but settles nothing.

records.title: The Effects of the Great Recession on Family Structure and Fertility
records.venue: The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science
records.note: Great Recession effects on FAMILY STRUCTURE and fertility together, with fertility down 9-11% and the family activated as an emergency support system. A macro shock moving both links at once; C.5.a owns the treatment.

records.title: The Effects of the Transition to Parenthood and Subsequent Children on Men’s Well-Being and Social Participation
records.note: Transition to fatherhood and men's wellbeing and social participation.

records.title: Elderly labor supply, endogenous grandparental childcare, and fertility in an OLG model
records.note: OLG model of grandparental childcare, elderly labour supply and fertility. C.2.a's exposure in a formal model.

records.title: CHAPTER NINE. Childrearing versus Childbearing: Coresidence of Mother and Child in Sub-Saharan Africa
records.note: No abstract. The title -- childrearing versus childbearing, co-residence of mother and child in sub-Saharan Africa -- names co-residence but of mother and CHILD, which is a different construct; not decidable from the title.

records.title: Grandparental Childcare and Second Birth in China: Evidence from a Dynamic Model and Empirical Study
records.note: GRANDPARENTAL CHILDCARE and SECOND BIRTH in China, dynamic model plus empirics. C.2.a's exposure with a parity-specific fertility outcome -- the closest boundary case in the batch, and one of at least three near-identical China second-birth childcare papers in this frame.

records.title: Grandparental childcare, family allowances and retirement policies
records.note: OLG model of grandparental childcare, child allowances and pension policy. Reclassified anchor; C.2.a's exposure.

records.title: Patrilines, patrilocality and fertility decline in Viet Nam
records.note: Patrilineal and PATRILOCAL family system against Vietnam's fertility decline and the resulting rise in sonless couples. The arrangement is systemic rather than varying across households, so identification is the question; full-text read.

records.title: Family Structure Differences in the Timing of Leaving Home: Exploring Mediating Factors
records.note: Eight-year panel event history of family structure against departure from the parental home, testing mediators including parent-child relationship quality and income. The best-identified link-1 study seen so far.

records.title: Multigenerational Households and the School Readiness of Children Born to Unmarried Mothers
records.note: MULTIGENERATIONAL HOUSEHOLDS and the school readiness of children born to unmarried mothers, framed as a policy alternative to marriage promotion. Arrangement as exposure, child development as outcome.

records.title: The timing of marriage vis-à-vis coresidence and childbearing in Europe and the United States
records.note: Links the TIMING OF MARRIAGE to CORESIDENCE and CHILDBEARING across European countries and the US, extending Holland's marriage typology. All three events in one framework, cross-nationally -- descriptive, but it is the map of the sequence the chapter has to explain.

records.title: The Association Between Grandparental Coresidence and Adolescent Childbearing
records.note: GRANDPARENTAL CO-RESIDENCE with adolescent women against early childbearing, finding co-residence DELAYS first birth beyond the teenage years. A pre-launch arrangement-to-birth estimate with A.23's predicted negative sign, in a configuration the scope did not enumerate -- three generations with the young woman as the pre-launch member.

records.title: Intergenerational exchanges in Vietnam: Family size, sex composition, and the location of children
records.note: Intergenerational support to elderly parents in Vietnam by family size and children's location; co-residence with married children is an outcome, support the object.

records.title: Grandmothers and Coresident Grandchildren
records.venue: Families in Society The Journal of Contemporary Social Services
records.note: Prevalence and duration of coresident grandmotherhood 1967-92. Exposure prevalence for the three-generation configuration flagged in batch 4.

records.title: Intergenerational co-residence and schooling
records.venue: The Journal of the Economics of Ageing
records.note: No abstract; intergenerational co-residence and SCHOOLING. Arrangement as exposure, education as outcome.

records.title: Fertility as an Adjustment to Risk *
records.note: Fertility as an adjustment to mortality risk. A.1's.

records.title: Someone to live for: social well-being, parenthood status, and decision-making in oncology.
records.note: Parenthood status and oncology treatment preferences.

records.title: Experiencing loneliness in parenthood: a scoping review
records.note: Scoping review of loneliness in parenthood.

records.title: Coresidence With Husband’s Parents, Labor Supply, and Duration to First Birth
records.note: THE EXTENDED ARM'S BEST RECORD. Duration to FIRST BIRTH among Taiwanese married women born 1933-68, treating CO-RESIDENCE WITH THE HUSBAND'S PARENTS and labour supply as ENDOGENOUS, with a full-information maximum-likelihood duration model with endogenous binary variables. It confronts §3's anticipation problem directly rather than controlling for it, and it separates the labour-supply channel the scope named as the largest route-out. Priority read.

records.title: Household division of labor and cross-country differences in household formation rates
records.note: No abstract; household division of labour and cross-country differences in HOUSEHOLD FORMATION RATES. A theory of link 1's cross-country variation, which is the pattern the pre-launch arm rests on.

records.title: The Differentiation of Multigenerational Households
records.venue: Canadian Journal on Aging / La Revue canadienne du vieillissement
records.note: Distinguishes multigenerational households located in the PARENT's home from those in the CHILD's home, and says the distinction carries the dependency direction. That is §6's wall stated by the field itself; read in full when the wall is written up.

records.title: THE TREND AND THE MODEL SCHEDULE OF LEAVING THE PARENTAL HOME AFTER MARRIAGE IN CHINA
records.note: Model schedule for leaving the parental home AFTER MARRIAGE in China -- the extended-couple to nuclear transition. Exposure trend, no fertility estimate.

records.title: Starting a Family at Your Parents’ House: Multigenerational Households and Below Replacement Fertility in Urban Bulgaria
records.note: Full-title version of the gated anchor: multigenerational households and below-replacement fertility in URBAN BULGARIA, contrasting Italy's postponement with Bulgaria's early childbearing under the same strong multigenerational links. The contrast is the chapter's own configuration problem stated as a finding -- the same arrangement produces opposite timing in two settings.

records.title: Patterns of lowest-low fertility in Europe
records.note: Billari and Kohler's lowest-low fertility analysis, relating period and cohort fertility to LEAVING THE PARENTAL HOME, marriage and female labour force participation. Aggregate and descriptive, but it puts the exposure and the outcome in one framework across countries.

records.title: Health and marital status of older Chinese couples and implications for intergenerational co-residence
records.note: Health and marital status of older Chinese couples and implications for intergenerational co-residence.

records.title: Counting on Potential Grandparents? Adult Children’s Entry Into Parenthood Across European Countries
records.note: 'Counting on POTENTIAL GRANDPARENTS?' -- whether would-be grandparents' PROPENSITY to care predicts adult children's ENTRY INTO PARENTHOOD across Europe, Demography. Uses the propensity rather than realised care, which is the same endogeneity fix as the living-status paper in batch 18. C.2.a's exposure, but the design is one this chapter should borrow.

records.title: Nest Leaving in Europe
records.note: No abstract; 'Nest Leaving in Europe' is squarely link 1 but the outcome is not visible.

records.title: ‘Banking time’: egg freezing and the negotiation of future fertility
records.note: Non-medical egg freezing. A.17's.

records.title: Teenage Mothers in Nuclear and Extended Households
records.note: Household arrangements OF adolescent mothers -- nuclear versus extended. Childbearing precedes and shapes the arrangement.

records.title: Parental Coresidence, Young Adult Role, Economic, and Health Changes, and Psychological Well-being
records.note: PARENTAL CORESIDENCE in young adulthood against psychological wellbeing, Add Health, with role, economic and health changes as mediators. The pre-launch exposure with a wellbeing outcome; the mediator set is close to §9's.

records.title: Shifting Parenthood to Advanced Reproductive Ages: Trends, Causes and Consequences
records.note: No abstract; shifting parenthood to advanced reproductive ages. A.15's.

records.title: Household Formation and Marriage Markets in Rural Areas
records.note: No abstract; preprint duplicate of the Handbook chapter on household formation and rural marriage markets.

records.title: Future fertility trends are shaped at the intersection of gender and social stratification
records.note: Same debate; gender and social stratification. D.2.a's.

records.title: Conceiving Parents Through Law
records.venue: International Journal of Law Policy and the Family
records.note: Legal parentage after assisted conception.

records.title: Determinants and characteristics of help provision for elderly people living at home and in relation to quality of life
records.note: Help provision to elderly people living at home.

records.title: Thai elderly who do not coreside with their children
records.note: No abstract; 'Thai elderly who do not coreside with their children' is decisive on the homonym.

records.title: A day late and a dollar short: Liquidity and household formation among student borrowers
records.note: No abstract; 'A day late and a dollar short: LIQUIDITY AND HOUSEHOLD FORMATION AMONG STUDENT BORROWERS' in the Journal of Financial Economics. C.3.g and C.3.e own the treatment, but it estimates a driver-to-arrangement link with finance-journal identification standards. Report to C.3.g; read for the design.

records.title: Reassessing the decline in parent-child old-age coresidence during the twentieth century
records.note: Twentieth-century decline in parent-child OLD-AGE co-residence, reassessed in life-years. The homonym, and a careful one.

records.title: Second-Generation Parenthood: A Panel Study of Grandmother and Grandchild Coresidency Among Low-Income Families, 1967-1992
records.venue: The Journal of Sociology & Social Welfare
records.note: Panel study of grandmother-grandchild co-residency among low-income families 1967-92. Prevalence and duration of the three-generation configuration; the arrangement is the outcome.

records.title: Pathways to a Stable Union? Pregnancy and Childbearing Among Cohabiting and Married Couples
records.note: No abstract; pregnancy and childbearing among cohabiting versus married couples. A.7's union-type question.

records.title: Young people leaving home
records.note: Qualitative study of 80 young Britons who left home before 21, covering courtship, family formation and single parenthood. No estimate but directly on the pre-launch mechanism.

records.title: Childlessness and union histories: evidence from Finnish population register data
records.note: Childlessness and UNION histories in Finnish register data. A.7's union variable; register quality is notable.

records.title: Do parents matter? Intergenerational ties and fertility preferences in a low-fertility context
records.note: 'Do parents matter?' Multidimensional INTERGENERATIONAL TIES against married women's intended and ideal family size in Jiangsu, an extremely low-fertility Chinese province. Directly on the extended arm's estimand, with the parents' own preferences among the measured dimensions -- which is the mechanism the mother-in-law records describe qualitatively.

records.title: Coresidence with mother-in-law and maternal anemia in rural India
records.note: No abstract; gated decoy. Co-residence with mother-in-law and maternal ANAEMIA in rural India -- the arrangement as exposure with a health outcome.

records.title: The Boomerang AGE
records.note: Book version of 'The Boomerang Age'; the pre-launch exposure trend as a monograph.

records.title: Parenthood, Stress, and Mental Health in Late Midlife and Early Old Age
records.venue: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.note: CO-RESIDENCE WITH ADULT CHILDREN as an 'off-time' parental role against parents' mental health in late midlife. The parents' side of the pre-launch arrangement, with wellbeing rather than fertility as the outcome -- the same framing as the Japanese cost-to-parents chapter.

records.title: Shipibo polygyny and patrilocality
records.note: Prevalence of polygyny and patrilocality in Shipibo villages as an index of cultural change; residence pattern is the outcome, not fertility.

records.title: Subsequent Fertility Among Teen Mothers: Longitudinal Analyses of Recent National Data
records.venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family
records.note: Subsequent fertility among teen mothers; the arrangement is not the exposure.

records.title: Childrearing Responsibility and Stepfamily Fertility in Finland and Austria
records.venue: European Journal of Population / Revue européenne de Démographie
records.note: No abstract; childrearing responsibility and STEPFAMILY fertility is a co-residence-with-children construct, not co-residence with parents.

records.title: Writing the names: Marriage style, living arrangements, and first birth interval in a Nepali society
records.note: Event-history analysis of the first-birth interval in Nepal with POSTMARITAL LIVING ARRANGEMENTS as the exposure, finding extended-household residence with reduced natal-kin contact matters and naming coital frequency as the mechanism. A direct arrangement-to-birth estimate, and it names the A.14 channel.

records.title: Teenage childbearing in Great Britain and the spatial concentration of poverty households
records.note: Area deprivation and teenage childbearing in Great Britain.

records.title: Women’s Retirement Intentions and Behavior: The Role of Childbearing and Marital Histories
records.venue: European Journal of Population / Revue européenne de Démographie
records.note: No abstract; childbearing and marital histories and women's retirement.

records.title: Chapter 51 Household Formation and Marriage Markets in Rural Areas
records.note: No abstract; Handbook of Development Economics chapter on household formation and rural marriage markets. Theory for link 1; duplicate of the RePEc preprint in batch 11.

records.title: An Old-Age Security Motive for Fertility in the United States?
records.note: Old-age security motive for fertility, estimating what a co-resident family contributes to elderly poverty alleviation. C.3.c's, and the co-residence here is the elder-support kind.

records.title: Fertility will be determined by the changing ideal family size and the empowerment to reach these targets
records.note: Same debate; ideal family size and empowerment.

records.title: Cross‐lagged Models of Marital Relationships and Intergenerational Conflicts during Transition to Parenthood: Effect of Patrilineal Coresidence
records.note: Cross-lagged models of marital relationships and intergenerational conflict across the TRANSITION TO PARENTHOOD, with the effect of PATRILINEAL CORESIDENCE. Co-residence as a moderator of what happens after a birth rather than a cause of it -- but the cross-lagged design is the closest thing in the extended arm to modelling the two directions at once.

records.title: Teenage childbearing and school dropout in a sample of 18,791 single mothers in Cameroon
records.note: Teenage childbearing and school dropout in Cameroon.

records.title: Young African-American Multigenerational Families in Poverty: Quality of Mothering and Grandmothering
records.note: Parenting quality in multigenerational African-American families; the arrangement is the setting and the outcome is mothering behaviour.

records.title: Relational contracts for household formation, fertility choice and separation
records.note: No abstract; relational contracts for household formation, fertility choice and separation. Formal theory linking the arrangement decision to fertility.

records.title: Son Preference in the Context of Fertility Decline: Limits to New Constructions of Gender and Kinship in Nepal
records.note: Son preference in patrilineal, patrilocal Nepal. D.2.c's.

records.title: Trends and transitions in children's coresidence with older adults in Beijing municipality
records.note: Trends in co-residence between older adults and adult children in Beijing. The homonym, with the arrangement as outcome.

records.title: Progress and Stagnation: Changes in Fertility and Women's Position in an Indian Village
records.note: Women's status, fertility and contraception in a Maharashtra village; the arrangement is not the exposure.

records.title: The Age at Leaving Home in the United States, 1850–1860
records.note: Age at leaving home in the United States 1850-60; historical link 1.

records.title: Factors associated with the timing and duration of the leaving-home stage of the family life cycle
records.note: Timing and duration of the leaving-home stage as a function of sibship composition and birth intervals. Australian data, no fertility outcome.

records.title: Health, social care and technological interventions to improve functional ability of older adults living at home: An evidence and gap map
records.note: Evidence and gap map on interventions for older adults living at home.

records.title: Fertility, household structure, and parental labor supply: Evidence from China
records.note: No abstract; the Journal of Comparative Economics version of the gated anchor 'Fertility, household structure, and parental labor supply: Evidence from China'. Keep this over the SSRN preprint.

records.title: Why do young adults coreside with their parents?
records.note: 'WHY DO YOUNG ADULTS CORESIDE WITH THEIR PARENTS?' in Real Estate Economics: nearly one in two US adults aged 18-29 now lives with parents against one in four in 1960, and a Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition identifies a role for HOUSING AFFORDABILITY against the labour-market and marriage-delay explanations. It decomposes the very trend the pre-launch arm rests on, and it puts Wall 1's variable in competition with the alternatives rather than assuming one. Second-read packet.

records.title: INTERGENERATIONAL PROXIMITY AND THE FERTILITY INTENTIONS OF MARRIED WOMEN
records.note: Gated anchor. Nationally representative surveys of married women in JAPAN AND ITALY, arguing that explanations of very low fertility in strong-family countries emphasise childrearing costs and ignore the offsetting influence of DISTINCTIVE LIVING ARRANGEMENTS. The proximity cell's core record, and it spans the two settings the two arms live in.

records.title: The decline in average family size and its implications for the average benefits of within‐household sharing
records.note: Declining family size and the lost benefits of within-household sharing, arguing projections ignore household formation. The economies-of-scale argument that makes co-residence attractive -- the mechanism running the other way from A.23's.

records.title: The design and content of the National Survey of Families and Households.
records.note: Procedural history of the NSFH survey design.

records.title: Racial Differences in the Determinants of the Coresidence of and Contacts Between Elderly Parents and Their Adult Children
records.note: Racial differences in intergenerational co-residence among people aged 74+. The homonym.

records.title: Instability in Parent–Child Coresidence and Adolescent Development in Urban South Africa
records.note: Instability in PARENT-CHILD co-residence and adolescent development in urban South Africa. The child's co-residence with a parent, and a development outcome.

records.title: Cultural Influences on the Timing of First Births in India: Large Differences that add up to Little Difference
records.note: Long first-birth intervals in North India after early marriage, with standard explanations rejected. Post-marital residence with in-laws is the usual candidate but the abstract does not say; full-text read.

records.title: Fostering Household Formation: Evidence from a Spanish Rental Subsidy
records.venue: The B E Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy
records.note: PUBLISHED VERSION of Aparicio-Fenoll and Oppedisano. Spain's 2008 monthly cash subsidy conditional on renting, DiD on the ELIGIBILITY AGE THRESHOLD, with living apart from parents, living with a partner AND CHILDBEARING as outcomes, larger for lower earners and in high-rent areas. The chapter's single identified pre-launch design; keep this over the SSRN preprints in batches 12 and 14.

records.title: Timing of parenthood in relation to other life transitions and adult social functioning
records.note: Timing of parenthood relative to other transitions and adult social functioning.

records.title: Patrilocality and Child Sex Ratios in India
records.note: No abstract; patrilocality and child sex ratios in India. D.2.c's.

records.title: Changes in diet through adolescence and early adulthood: longitudinal trajectories and association with key life transitions
records.venue: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
records.note: LEAVING HOME among four early-adulthood transitions against changes in diet. Arrangement as exposure, diet as outcome.

records.title: The Impact of Early-Life Debt on Household Formation: An Empirical Investigation of Homeownership, Marriage and Fertility
records.venue: OhioLink ETD Center (Ohio Library and Information Network)
records.note: Early-life debt -- college loans and credit card balances -- against HOMEOWNERSHIP, MARRIAGE AND FERTILITY after leaving college, Survey of Consumer Finances. C.3.g owns the treatment, but it estimates the household-formation chain through to a birth in one dataset, which is the structure this chapter is short of. Report to C.3.g and read.

records.title: Does coresidence with grandparents reduce the negative association between sibship size and reading test scores? Evidence from 40 countries
records.venue: Research in Social Stratification and Mobility
records.note: No abstract; co-residence with grandparents and reading scores across 40 countries. Child outcome.

records.title: Multigenerational Households: A Descriptive Approach to Distinctive Definitions
records.note: No abstract; 'MULTIGENERATIONAL HOUSEHOLDS: A Descriptive Approach to Distinctive Definitions'. A definitional paper on the exposure -- directly useful for §9's ARRANGEMENT_MEASURE and §6's configuration split. Trace.

records.title: Family reproduction and stem-family system: From Pyrenean valleys to Norwegian farms
records.note: Comparative study of two stem-family systems, Pyrenean and Norwegian, where the house is continued through non-egalitarian inheritance. Pre-modern; A.7's under Ruling 2, and the clearest statement of how a stem system ties household continuity to reproduction.

records.title: Wealth modifies relationships between kin and women's fertility in high-income countries
records.note: WEALTH MODIFIES the relationship between kin and women's fertility in high-income countries -- a moderator result on the extended arm's mechanism. Exposure is kin presence and support rather than the arrangement, so C.2.a's, but the heterogeneity finding matters for the extended arm's transportability.

records.title: Linked lives: The utility of an agent-based approach to modeling partnership and household formation in the context of social care
records.note: Agent-based model of partnership and household formation for social-care supply.

records.title: Education, Labor Force Participation and Changing Fertility Patterns. A Study of Women and Socioeconomic Change in Twentieth Century Sweden.
records.note: Women's education and labour force participation against fertility in twentieth-century Sweden. C.2.e's.

records.title: Regional Differences in the Transition to Adulthood
records.venue: The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science
records.note: Living arrangements of 15-35 year olds in Europe and the US, identifying a Southern European pattern of extended stay in the parental home with DIRECT transitions from home to marriage and PARENTHOOD, against Northern and US patterns. records.title: The Constitution of Parenthood
records.note: No abstract; 'The Constitution of Parenthood', legal.
records.recovered_abstract: This Article challenges the conventional assumption that the Constitution protects only biological parent-child relationships and makes an affirmative case for constitutional protection for nonbiological parents. Family law in a growing number of states legally recognizes nonbiological parents in a range of families—including nonmarital families, families headed by same-sex couples, and families formed through assisted reproduction. But in some states, nonbiological parents who have not adopted are treated as legal strangers to their children. When these parents turn to the Constitution to assert a liberty interest in their parent-child relationship, they find no relief. Courts conclude that only biological parents possess a right to parental recognition protected by the Due Process Clause. This biological understanding of constitutional parenthood often rests on a reading of Supreme Court precedents from the 1970s and 1980s involving the rights of unmarried fathers and the status of foster parents. This Article revisits those precedents—both to show that they present a more complicated approach to parenthood than conventionally assumed and to make clear the ways in which they are in tension with more recent constitutional commitments. Rather than elaborate a biological approach to parenthood, the Court’s decisions on unmarried fathers and foster parents view parenthood as a social practice. Even as these precedents provide useful insights about parenthood’s social dimensions, they are outdated. Decided decades ago, these decisions condone forms of inequality that now appear constitutionally suspect. Since they were decided, legal understandings of the family have shifted significantly. The Court itself has contributed to the changing legal landscape through its decisions on the constitutional rights of same-sex couples—who ordinarily include nonbiological parents.<br><br>Today, insights, principles, and values observable in constitutional precedents on parenthood and the family point toward a liberty interest in parental recognition that reaches nonbiological parents. To show how, this Article turns to contemporary family-law developments. Modern family law takes from constitutional precedents important insights about parenthood and yet updates the meanings and implications of those precedents. Family law’s functional turn has featured the vindication of nonbiological parent-child bonds based in part on interpretations of constitutional decisions on unmarried fathers, foster parents, and same-sex couples. In valuing established parent-child bonds in marital and nonmarital families, in different-sex and same-sex couples, and for men and women, family-law authorities have found support in the Court’s decisions but have taken those decisions in more inclusive and egalitarian directions. Even as this functional vision of parenthood has arisen as a formal matter in family law, it reflects and extends important constitutional commitments in ways that shed light on the parent-child relationships that merit recognition as a matter of due process. Ultimately, constitutional understandings of parenthood may evolve in light of insights from family law. This Article’s examination of the law of parenthood contributes to an account of the dialogic relationship between family law and constitutional law—demonstrating how family-law authorities develop approaches to the family that draw on and apply constitutional principles in ways constitutional decisionmakers may eventually adopt.

records.recovered_abstract: This paper investigates the role of childcare provided by grandparents for the fertility decisions of their offspring. We exploit a decade of pension reforms in Italy that mandated the grandparental generation to a working horizon longer than they would have had otherwise. We argue that the rise in retirement age meant a negative shock to the supply of informal childcare for the next generation.Our results show that one additional grandparent available in the early child-bearing years increases by about five percent the number of children. We show that the fertility effects of delayed retirement are limited to close-knits with a strong familistic structure. The result is not just the mechanical consequence of delayed exit from parental home, of more investment in education or of more attachment to the labour market. In light of the Italian lowest low fertility we conclude that pension reforms may have had unintended inter-generational effects. This conclusion is consistent with the sharp drop in total fertility documented by official statistics for the most conservative areas of the country.

records.recovered_abstract: This paper considers the role of grandparental childcare in China’s extraordinarily high female labor-market participation rate. Indeed, the high female labor-market participation and low labor-income penalty for childbirth is all the more remarkable given the lack of public subsidies for childcare. Using a novel and high-quality dataset, we find that childcare provided by retired grandparents significantly reduces the duration of career breaks for young women and helps women remain in the labor force. We further show that well-educated urban women benefit most from grandparental childcare, especially in the first three years of the child’s life before there is a possibility to enter kindergarten.

records.recovered_abstract: The Australian Government Department of Families, Housing, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs commissioned the Social Policy Research, Evaluation and Analysis Centre to report on how a young person’s future is shaped by his or her investments in education and choice of career path during early adulthood. This report describes whether young Australians from different family backgrounds are economically supported by their parents and how this support, or the lack of it, correlates with their decisions about educational and labour market investments. The report distinguishes between two kinds of parental support: co-residence and financial transfers. The analysis contributes to the literature on identifying young people at risk and can inform policies targeted at assisting young people in need and policies intended to counter the intergenerational transmission of disadvantage. The report begins with a review of the previous literature. The evidence suggests that young people in Australia are increasingly dependent on their parents for support as they complete their education and enter the labour market. Recent cohorts are less likely to leave home, more likely to receive financial support from their parents when they do live apart, and more likely to return home as circumstances change. This is partly because it now takes substantially longer than it once did to acquire work skills, and partly because of changes in social policy which have shifted the burden of supporting young adults from the public purse to families. The report provides new evidence based on analysis of Youth in Focus (YIF) Survey data combined with Centrelink’s administrative data about each family’s receipt of income support while the young person was growing up. Survey data were collected from a cohort of young Australians who were 18 years of age in 2006. The young people were interviewed about their current circumstances in 2006 and again in 2008. In 2006, YIF also interviewed their mothers, who provided additional information about circumstances during the young people’s childhood. The report uses the parents’ history of receipt of income support (Centrelink data) as a measure of the family’s social and economic disadvantage. The analysis is divided into two main parts. The first part is descriptive and gives an overview of young people’s study, work activities, the support they receive from their parents in the form of co-residence or financial transfers and, finally, how activities and support vary for people of different family backgrounds. The second part presents regression results from the estimation of models of co-residence, financial transfer, study activity and work activity. The regressions control for other background variables such as parents’ education, occupation, birth country, family size and family structure. Regarding the relationship between parental support and youth activities, the main findings can be summarised as follows. Young people who continue to live with their parents receive fewer financial transfers than otherwise similar young people who live apart, so there appears to be a trade-off in the support provided through co-residence versus financial transfers. Conditional on the youths’ study and employment status, parents direct larger financial transfers towards their children who are not living at home or who are studying full time, and away from their children who are working full time, so financial support appears to be more targeted at age 20 than at age 18. Looking at youths’ activities, enrollment in post-secondary education is not closely related to co-residential support, but is positively related to financial support. In contrast, youths’ employment status seems to depend on co-residence, but not on parental financial transfers. Specifically, youths who continue to live with their parents are significantly more likely to work part time and are significantly less likely to be unemployed or out of the labour market entirely. Regarding the role of family background and socioeconomic disadvantage, the main findings are as follows. Young people growing up in families with a history of receiving income support are less likely to live at home. Eighteen-year-olds from families who have a history of relying on income support receive less financial support from their parents, and the disparity in the financial support provided by families that do and do not have a history of receiving income support is larger at age 20 than at age 18. There is no significant effect of a family history of income support receipt on young people’s student status at either age 18 or age 20 once we account for family background, parental income, parental support (both co-residence and financial transfers) and youths’ employment status. Having a family history of income support receipt at age 18 is associated with a lower probability of part-time employment and a higher probability of unemployment or non-participation, but these relationships are much weaker at age 20.

records.recovered_abstract: This paper tests the effects of fertility on household structure and parental labor supply in rural China. To solve the endogeneity problem, we use a unique survey on households with twin children and a comparison group of non-twin households. The ordinary least squares estimates show a negative correlation between fertility and parental labor supply. Using twinning as a natural experiment, we do not find evidence on the negative effects of fertility on parental labor supply. By contrast, we find that the twinning-induced increase in fertility enhances significantly the coresidence of grandparents. The results remain robust when we use the Chinese 1990 population census. We suggest that the negative effects of fertility on parental labor supply are mitigated by the childcare provided by grandparents. Our results have important implications for population and public childcare policies.

records.recovered_abstract: BACKGROUND The gap between improvements in women’s socioeconomic status and gender inequality at home has been offered as one explanation for very low fertility. Related empirical evidence is lacking for East Asian countries, where women may face particular challenges combining career and family due to unique regional contexts. OBJECTIVES This paper provides an up-to-date picture of Korean women’s fertility intentions and fertility behaviour, and of the division of their domestic labour with husbands, parents(-in-law), and formal childcare services. In addition, it examines how the informal and formal help women receive affects their fertility behavior. METHODS Using data from the 2008, 2010, and 2012 waves of the Korean Longitudinal Survey of Women and Families, I describe fertility intentions, fertility behaviour, and the labour division, and, focusing on women with one child, use logit regressions to estimate how various sources of help relate to the intended and unintended births of second children. RESULTS Particularly among women with one child, both fertility intentions and behaviour displayed greater variability, and fertility intentions were a good predictor of fertility behaviour. Husbands did not provide much help, and gender inequality grew with parity. As for intended births, husbands’ help increased their likelihood. Formal help also had a positive impact when its costs were not high, but parental help showed no significant impact. None of these sources of help was related to unintended births. CONCLUSION AND CONTRIBUTION To tackle Korea’s low fertility, the government policies would be wise to target women with one child. Empirical evidence from Korea supports the recent theoretical literature on the association of low fertility with gender inequity. Various sources of support that relieve women’s domestic labour burden and enhance their work-life compatibility may boost fertility rates in East Asia.

records.recovered_abstract: Young adults leave their parents' home at a higher rate in Northern Europe and the United States than in Southern Europe, with broad implications on labor mobility, intergenerational sharing of resources and on fertility. This paper assesses if differences in household structure can be traced back to restricted access to credit for the young. To study the causal impact of getting a loan on the probability of leaving the nest, we exploit two reforms of a Portuguese program that subsidized interest rate on mortgages signed by low- and medium-income young adults. Using a unique dataset that merges a Labor Force Survey with administrative debt records, we estimate that getting a mortgage loan increases the rate of leaving home by between 31 and 54 percentage points. We combine those estimates with an European household panel to document that if our preferred estimates held for all countries, differential use of credit markets would explain between 16% and 20% of the North-South differences in home leaving.

records.recovered_abstract: South Korea has undergone profound family transformations over the past five decades, marked by delayed marriage, rapid fertility decline, and rising divorce amid compressed socioeconomic change. Despite extensive scholarship on demographic trends, much less is known about how intergenerational living arrangements have evolved in this context. Using 1% microdata from the Korean censuses (1975–2020), this study examines changes in intergenerational coresidence from both the children’s and parents’ perspective, distinguishing patterns by marital status and exploring variations by age, gender, and educational attainment. We further apply decomposition techniques to disentangle behavioral and compositional contributions to overall trends. Results reveal a shifting nature of intergenerational coresidence: the traditional pattern of married children living with parents has nearly disappeared, driven by both behavioral and compositional changes, while the growing share of unmarried adults has given rise to “two-adult-generation” households. Korea thus exemplifies both transformation and continuity in intergenerational living. These findings call for a reconceptualization of intergenerational coresidence amid Korea’s rapid demographic and social transformation.

records.recovered_abstract: This study investigates the effect of grandparental childcare on the second birth in China when considering the mediating role of maternal labor participation, drawing on the China Migrants Dynamic Survey in 2016. By controlling sample selection bias and endogeneity with an endogenous switching Probit regression model, our analysis finds that grandparental childcare of the first child has a positive and significant effect on the second birth regardless of whether the mother participates in the labor market or not. To further understand how the positive effect comes to be, we make a mediation analysis which demonstrates the mediating effect of maternal labor force participation. It indicates a significant and negative effect of grandparenting on the second birth through promoting maternal employment. However, due to the positive, direct effect of the grandparental childcare on the second birth, the total effect is still positive.

records.recovered_abstract: The Nordic countries have remarkably high participation rates of mothers and a moderate decrease of fertility rates compared to other western countries. This has been attributed to the fact that the welfare state model and, especially, the family friendly policies chosen in the Nordic countries are unique. The availability of generous parental leave schemes including high compensation rates makes it possible for mothers to take a considerable time out of work in connection with childbirths and to return to their previous jobs afterwards, thanks to the high provision of public daycare. In this paper we evaluate family-friendly policies in the &apos;Nordic model&apos; with respect to the two modes of child care i.e. either parental care facilitated by maternal and parental leave schemes or non-parental publicly provided care. Our questions for discussion are: Is there a &apos;Nordic model&apos;, and is it worth the cost if effects on child development and welfare are included? Is there a trade-off between family-friendly policies and family welfare, and are there serious negative boomerang effects of family-friendly policies on womens position in the labor market? Is the &apos;Nordic model&apos; a model to aspire to?

records.recovered_abstract: This article analyses the extent to which changes in household composition over the life course affect the gender division of labour. It identifies and analyses cross-country disparities between France, Italy, Sweden and United States, using most recent data available from the Time Use National Surveys. We focus on gender differences in the allocation of time between market work, domestic work and leisure over the life-cycle. In order to map the life-cycle, we distinguish between nine key cross-country comparable life stages according to age and family structure such as exiting parental home, union formation, parenthood, and retiring from work. By using appropriate regression techniques (Tobit with selection, Tobit and OLS), we show large discrepancies in the gender division of labour at the different life stages. This gender gap exists in all countries at any stage of the life course, but is usually smaller at the two ends of the age distribution, and larger with parenthood. Beyond social norms, the impact of parenthood on time allocation varies across countries, being smaller in those where work-family balance policies are more effective and traditionally well-established.

records.recovered_abstract: In Southern Europe youngsters leave the parental home significantly later than in Northern Europe and United States. In this paper, we study the effect of a monthly cash subsidy on young adults&apos; emancipation, family formation, and fertility. The subsidy, introduced in Spain in 2008, is conditional on young adults renting accommodation, and it amounts to almost 20 percent of the average youngsters&apos; wage. Our identification strategy exploits the subsidy eligibility age threshold to assess the causal impact of the cash transfer. Difference-in-Differences and Regression Discontinuity estimates show that the policy increases emancipation rates by 0.9-2.3 percentage points, couple cohabitation by 1.2-2.4 percentage points, and the probability of having children by 4.8-8.1 percentage points for 22 year-olds compared to 21 year-olds. The effect is larger among young adults earning lower incomes and living in high rental price areas. This is consistent with the hypothesis that youngsters delay emancipation and family formation because they are budget constrained.

records.recovered_abstract: Female post-childbirth labor market participation and labor intensity are extraordinarily high in China, given that public childcare subsidies are limited and supportive policies for childbearing female employees are largely absent. Establishing a panel dataset that tracks female employment and childbirth, we find that such a paradox is well-explained by the intra-family childcare support provided by grandparents. Correcting the selection bias that stems from women’s fertility choices using the propensity score matching difference-in-difference model, we find that women without grandparental support suffer a substantial drop in post-childbirth employment, while women with grandparental support even experience a rise in employment after childbirth. It takes women without grandparental support twice as long to recover their employment after childbirth. Finally, we find that childbirth does not decrease women's labor intensity due to a lack of labor market flexibility, and that women face a stay-or-quit dilemma when grandparental childcare support is absent.

records.title: Conceiving Parents
records.note: No abstract; 'Conceiving Parents', legal.
records.recovered_abstract: This article revisits the contested question of parentage determination upon a child’s birth and argues that the relationship between prospective parents should be a factor in recognizing or refusing to recognize an individual as a parent. According to this approach, whether the pertinent parties were involved in a committed long-term relationship or merely hooked up, or the child’s conception was the result of rape, should be considered as part of the decision regarding the status of each of them as a legal parent. Existing laws and legal scholarship have focused either on biology or on intent, but have overlooked relationships. <br><br>This article does not suggest that relationships between potential joint parents be the only factor determining parentage. Rather, it suggests that relationships be considered together with two other considerations — biology and intent — in all cases of at-birth parentage determination, regardless of the “method” of conception, be it sex-based or through Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART). <br><br>Beyond the specific proposals for making parentage determinations, this article offers a vision of legal parenthood as an “all or nothing” indissoluble relationship. The perception of parenthood has been diluted over the last few decades as a side-effect of the (desirable in itself) erosion of parental exclusivity and the disaggregation of parental rights and responsibilities that followed. This article suggests that the erosion of parental status all-inclusiveness and permanence contradicts children's interests. In order to restore the meaning of parenthood as an enduring commitment, it argues that at-birth parentage determination should confer upon legal parents all the duties, responsibilities, privileges, and rights associated with parenthood, regarding both their vertical relationship with the child and their horizontal relationship with a co-parent, when there is one.

records.recovered_abstract: As with state recognized voluntary acknowledgements of parentage (VAPs) and state recognized assisted reproduction pacts (SRARPs) on childcare parentage for future or current children, state parent registries (PRs), often labeled putative paternity registries or putative father registries, embody declarations of expecting or current legal parenthood. Yet declarations on children in PRs often involve unilateral assertions, unlike dual parenthood declarations in VAPs or SRARPs. Actual parenthood under law for many PR declarants is never recognized because there are no simultaneous assertions by a second expecting or existing legal parent on the declarant’s parenthood, as with an assertion by an expecting or existing birth mother in a VAP or a SRARP.<br><br>PRs are further limited. They generally provide that those who register receive notice and an opportunity to be heard in any later adoption and/or parental rights termination proceeding involving a child to be born or born to another. Thus, the expecting and existing legal parenthood interests of PR declarants are protected in only discrete settings. PRs, for example, generally do not prompt a notice/hearing opportunity in any later probate or tort proceeding containing parentage issues.<br><br>In addition, PR opportunities are not explicitly afforded to all expecting and existing legal parents whose children are or may be subject to adoptions or parental rights termination proceedings. PR laws are often limited to "paternity" or "father" registrations even though adoption and termination proceedings can also foreclose nonpaternity and nonfather parental interests (contingent or current). <br><br>State laws should be reformed so that asserted parental rights/interests in PRs can be employed in more settings. As well, PR opportunities should be expanded to reflect the evolving legal changes recognizing increased parenthood opportunities for those with no biological or formal adoptive ties, including both women and men.<br><br>As current state PRs often follow the suggestions of the Uniform Law Commissioners (ULC) in their 1973, 2000 (as amended in 2002), and/or 2017 Uniform Parentage Acts (UPAs) and the American Law Institute (ALI) in its 2000 Principles of the Law of Family Dissolution: Analysis and Recommendations (2000 ALI Principles), and should soon follow the ALI Restatement Draft on Children and the Law (ALI Restatement Draft), the ULC and ALI pronouncements on PRs will first be explored. Then, the variations and limitations in state PRs will be surveyed, demonstrating how PR uses are limited and how PR opportunities for some expecting/existing legal parents are unavailable. Finally, suggestions are offered on reforming PRs to meet both constitutional and public policy concerns. Expansions are suggested on who can utilize PRs and on how PRs can be used.

records.title: The Quality of Life and Mortality Risk of Elderly People in Rural China: The Role of Family Support
records.note: No abstract; family support and elderly mortality risk in rural China.
records.recovered_abstract: The elderly share of China’s population is projected to grow well beyond the capacity of the nation’s social security system. Meanwhile, family care is being challenged by a decline in fertility and an increase in migration from rural to urban areas. This paper examines the short-, mid-, and long-term effects of family support on elderly well-being in rural China, using four-wave panel data on 1,456 persons aged 60 and above in the Chaohu region of China. Findings showed that compared with living alone, being coresident with others lowered the mortality risk of several chronic diseases; but being coresident with adult children increased the mortality risk of cardiovascular diseases, though it was associated with a higher quality of life in the short and middle term. Children’s educational attainment and financial support increased the quality of life except for an increased risk of new incidence of cardiovascular disease in the middle term.

records.recovered_abstract: Fertility rates in many developed countries have fallen to historically low levels, renewing attention to the constraints that shape reproductive decision-making. In Spain, low fertility is closely tied to reduced progression beyond the first child, making fertility intentions among parents especially important. This paper builds upon Rutigliano and Lozano (2022) by revisiting the relationship between grandparental childcare support and short-term fertility intentions using nationally representative data from the 2018 Spanish Fertility Survey. It extends their study by applying a Beckerian constraint-based framework and by centering the distinction between co-residential and non-residential support in the explanation of gendered differences in fertility intentions. Using gender-stratified logistic regression models across a series of specifications, the analysis finds that grandparental support is positively associated with short-term fertility intentions among Spanish parents aged 18-45 with at least one biological child in the household. Among women, only non-residential grandparental support is associated with higher fertility intentions. Among men, the positive association is concentrated among fathers receiving co-residential support, particularly those with two or more children; because the male co-residential subgroup is small, small-sample diagnostics suggest a reasonably robust but imprecisely estimated association. These findings contribute to research on low fertility by showing that informal intergenerational support should not be treated as a uniform resource: its association with fertility intentions varies by gender, parity, and household arrangement.

records.title: College as a Marriage Market
records.note: No abstract; 'College as a Marriage Market'. C.7.a's.
records.recovered_abstract: College graduates tend to marry each other. We use detailed Norwegian data to show that strong assortativity further arises by institution and field of study, especially among high earners from elite programs. Admission discontinuities reveal that enrollment itself, rather than selection, primarily drives matching by institution and field among the college-educated, and that these matches can be economically consequential. Elite professional programs, in particular, propel marginally admitted women into elite household formation: they earn substantially more themselves and match with higher-earning elite partners, becoming much more likely to join the top percentiles of household earnings while also reducing fertility. Marginal elite admission for men yields no change in partner earnings or fertility. College matchmaking effects are concentrated among students who attend the same institution at the same time, and are larger when opposite-sex peers are more abundant, indicating search costs in the marriage market.

records.title: Delayed Retirement, Intergenerational Childcare, and the Equilibrium Fertility Rate: An Analysis Based on an Extended OLG Model
records.note: No abstract; delayed retirement, intergenerational childcare and equilibrium fertility in an OLG model.
records.recovered_abstract: To address the persistent decline in fertility and the potential conflict between delayed retirement and fertility-support policies in China, this paper develops a dynamic general equilibrium overlapping-generations (OLG) model that incorporates delayed retirement, family and social childcare, and other fertility-related factors. We show that delayed retirement affects the equilibrium fertility rate through two channels. First, it reduces grandparental childcare time, thereby generating a negative effect on fertility. Second, it alters individuals’ intertemporal income ratio, thereby exerting an income effect whose direction depends on the relative elasticities of the total replacement rate and the inverse dependency ratio with respect to the delayed retirement age. Numeric simulations for China indicate that, with the delayed retirement age less than 10 years, the elasticity of the total replacement rate remains relatively high, thereby ensuring a positive income effect. However, because the current elasticity of substitution between grandparental and parental childcare in China is excessively high, this positive income effect is dominated by the negative grandparental-childcare effect. Consequently, a non-zero optimal delayed retirement age does not exist under prevailing conditions. This outcome not only suppresses the equilibrium fertility rate but also undermines effective coordination between delayed retirement and fertility-support policies. Therefore, reliance on grandparental childcare should be reduced, and the total replacement rate and the inverse dependency ratio should be appropriately adjusted so that the conditions supporting a non-zero optimal delayed retirement age can be established and gradually strengthened. Once a non-zero optimal delayed retirement age emerges, it can be progressively increased toward the target statutory retirement age under the current delayed retirement policy, thereby transforming the previously adverse policy interaction into a mutually reinforcing and coordinated state.

records.title: How Do Children Affect the Need to Save for Retirement?
records.note: No abstract; children and retirement saving.
records.recovered_abstract: Children consume a substantial portion of a household’s income while living at home, but are usually financially independent by the time the parents reach retirement age. Relatively little attention has been paid to how children affect parents’ need to save for retirement. In this paper I use expenditure data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics to construct life cycle expenditure patterns from households with children and childless households, comparing the two to gain insights on how children affect household consumption and how these differences may affect retirement planning strategies for parents versus childless adults. For households who had children, expenditures from ages 65 through 69 are 3 percent lower than from ages 45 to 49, while for childless households expenditures rise 33 percent from ages 45 to 49 through ages 65-69. Similarly, parental household expenditures at age 65-69 are equal to about 80 percent of earnings from ages 45-49, versus 94 percent for nonparental households. These life cycle expenditure patterns appear sufficiently distinct that both households planning for retirement and analysts evaluating the adequacy of household retirement saving should consider the presence of children in the household as a factor affecting the wealth necessary for retirees to maintain their pre-retirement standard of living in retirement.

records.title: The Long-term Consequences of Fertility on the Elderly’s Labor Supply
records.note: No abstract; long-term consequences of fertility on elderly labour supply.
records.recovered_abstract: Two trends are shaping the demographic structure in China in recent decades: population ageing and declining fertility. This paper explores the long-term effect of fertility on the elderly’s labor supply in China. By applying the instrumental variable methods on the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) dataset, I find that having more children decreases the elderly’s labor supply, especially for the disadvantaged elderly, including females, those living in rural regions and those with low levels of educational attainment. The negative effect is concentrated on the effect on the extensive margin of labor supply, rather than the intensive margin. I rule out co-residence with adult children and providing care to grandchildren as potential channels for the negative effect on the elderly’s labor supply. The increase in the net transfer from children as the number of children increases can be a viable explanation for the negative effect. The linkage between fertility and labor supply of the elderly has important policy implications.

records.title: How Does Digital Life Affect Family Fertility Behavior? — An Analysis Based on CFPS Data of Chinese Families with a Second Child
records.note: No abstract; digital life and second-child fertility behaviour in CFPS. C.2.h's.
records.recovered_abstract: This paper uses data from the 2014–2020 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) and draws on Becker’s household production theory to examine the impact of digital life on second-child fertility behavior. The results show that digital life has a significant negative effect on second-child fertility: households with higher levels of digital engagement are less likely to have a second child. Digital life influences fertility mainly through three channels: time displacement, parenting pressure, and changes in parenting attitudes. Among different dimensions of digital life, digital learning, work, and entertainment exert a stronger negative impact on fertility than digital consumption. The negative effect of digital life is more pronounced after the implementation of the universal two-child policy, in urban households, in higher-income families, and in families whose first child is a boy. Moreover, the crowding-out effect of healthcare coverage and the rising cost of childrearing further strengthen this negative impact. However, modern parenting attitudes and grandparental childcare support can partially mitigate this adverse effect. Based on these findings, this paper proposes a series of policy recommendations aimed at improving digital life management and optimizing household fertility behavior.

records.recovered_abstract: <div> <div> <div> <p><span>Fertility has fallen sharply in China and South Korea, and this paper documents a parallel decline among Chinese and Korean Americans living in a markedly different socioeconomic environment. Using ACS and administrative birth records (NVSS) for 2008–2024, I characterize where this decline is located within the U.S. household life cycle. Age-standardized fertility rates among Chinese and Korean American women aged 25–44 fell by approximately 41 and 26 percent between 2016 and 2024, substan- tially more than among the principal U.S. comparison groups. Partnership measures changed by similar small magnitudes across Chinese and Korean women and the non- Hispanic white BA+ benchmark group, locating the fertility divergence after household formation. Within early marriage, the decline is disproportionately concentrated among coethnic dual-college couples. The Chinese triple-difference relative to the analogous non-Hispanic white cell is </span><span>−</span><span>4</span><span>.</span><span>6 </span><span>percentage points, with the largest movement in 2023– 2024; the Korean differential is economically large but less precisely estimated. Within the focal cell, Chinese declines appear among U.S.-born, childhood-arrival, and adult- arrival women, making changing composition among recent adult immigrants an insuf- ficient explanation. The results do not identify a causal mechanism, but they locate a recent diaspora fertility decline at the marriage-to-birth margin and in households plausibly most exposed to intensive child-investment and dual-career pressures.&nbsp;</span></p> </div> </div> </div>

records.title: Delay in Marriage and Income Inequality in Japan: The Impact of the Increased Number of Unmarried Adults Living with Their Parents on the Household
records.note: No abstract; preprint of the Japanese 'parasite singles' paper below.
records.recovered_abstract: The continuous decline in the fertility rate has been witnessed since 1980 in Japan. Japan's total fertility rate in 2005 is 1.32, which is far below the replacement rate, 2.08. One of the main reasons for declining the fertility rate is the delay in marriage or even shy away from marriage among young adults. In this paper, looking at youth in terms of their relation to the household, we will examine the economic disparities of unmarried adults living with their parents in Japan in comparative perspective with Europe and U.S. The countries which I analyze in this paper are France, Germany, Italy, Sweden, U.K., U.S., and Taiwan, compared with Japan. The paper consists of two parts. First, I will examine economic disparities among households with unmarried adults, and second, the determinants of co-residence with their parents will be scrutinized. The degree of the Japanese youth unemployment rate is not as high as those in European countries, but it is commonly found that the youth tend to be targeted by economic downturns, and that they are exposed to high economic risk. Young unmarried people do not always live alone, but share their households with their family, mostly their parents. Less than 20 percent of unmarried adults live alone in Japan, and in Italy and Taiwan, its corresponding figures are even lower than that in Japan. The proportion of income derived from unmarried adults in the household economy is more or less negatively associated with family income. Therefore, unmarried adults are not always dependent on their parents in the household but there are cases in which unmarried adults are the ones who support the family income by living with their parents, particularly in low-income groups. The economic role of unmarried adult children in the household differs by the level of household economy. In determining if unmarried adults live with their parents, the economic factor is important for both men and women. Since their individual income is not high enough to have their independent households, they stay in their parental home. The most interesting finding in this analysis is on the gender role in living arrangement with their parents. Unmarried female adults are less likely to stay in their parental home if their mothers are at work, while there is no significant impact of mother’s work on their male counterparts. Unmarried daughters are like to be expected to take over the mother's role in the households when she is in the labor force, so there is a gendered allocation of family role for unmarried adults. Thus, the economic levels of unmarried adults and the gender constrain in allocating family roles were important in determining the living arrangement with the parents.

records.note: No abstract; family formation under a subjective future constraint. D.3.c-adjacent. | RA GATE RE-READ: The abstract places HOUSEHOLD FORMATION and housing markets among the margins the paper synthesises, and proposes subjective future evaluation as the underdeveloped one. Theory bearing on this chapter's link 1, and a D.3.c seam.
records.recovered_abstract: Population economics has developed powerful models of marriage, fertility, and household formation. These models show how income, prices, education, child costs, time constraints, bargaining, housing markets, and family policy shape demographic behavior. Yet they leave underdeveloped a margin that is increasingly central to explaining declining fertility, delayed marriage, and weaker household formation: how people evaluate the future into which family commitments are made. After synthesizing this literature and the canonical models, I introduce the concept of a subjective future constraint. Family formation requires more than material affordability and temporal feasibility; it also requires a sufficiently favorable subjective assessment of the future to justify durable, long-horizon commitments. This constraint can be measured using subjective well-being, especially future life evaluation. I then outline an empirical agenda for population economics that integrates subjective well-being measures into models of fertility, household formation, labor markets, and macroeconomic equilibrium.

records.note: No abstract; 'Happiness in Old Age: The Daughter Connection'.
records.recovered_abstract: Family and intergenerational relationships are becoming increasingly important as sources of support and care for the elderly population in the rapidly aging Asian societies. However, this has also raised concern over the reinforcement of cultural preferences for sons as a source of old-age security. This paper, therefore, revisits the determinants of happiness in old age by investigating the role of adult children&apos;s gender in the context of Thailand, an aging Asian country with no legacy of sex preference in fertility. We employ nationally representative data to examine the association between old-age happiness and the presence of a coresiding child. Compared with living alone, living with at least one child is found to be positively associated with older persons&apos; happiness. However, this result is specific to daughters. Moreover, compared with older men, older women systematically benefit from a "daughter effect." Coresiding daughters with a university education and those who maintain a good relationship with their parents help explain the positive happiness effect on older persons. Coresiding daughters are shown to increase the happiness of their parents through three channels: reducing loneliness, improving self-rated health, and improving the economic conditions of older parents.
