records.recovered_abstract: The fifty-year infrastructure transition documented in prior papers in this series did not affect all American households equally. It restructured material conditions along infrastructure-layer lines, generating systematically divergent household trajectories that conventional family sociology attributes to cultural, moral, or ethnic factors. This paper develops the cultural materialist argument that the mode of reproduction-fertility, marriage, household formation, and intergenerational wealth transmission-is downstream of the mode of production. Analyzed through the lens of the eight-coalition framework and supported by Census CPS, PSID, and GSS data, the paper makes five claims. First, family structure variation-delayed marriage, declining fertility, single-parent households, rising childlessness-tracks infrastructure-layer position more closely than it tracks ethnicity, religion, or geography once layer is controlled. Second, within every major racial and ethnic group, reproductive outcomes diverge by infrastructure layer: infrastructure position, not group membership, is the organizing variable. Third, the American welfare state operates as two parallel systems with opposite visibility architectures: an invisible system of immunities and privileges serving FIRE/Networked households, and a visible, stigmatized system of claim-rights serving Manufacturing/Extractive households. Fourth, the analysis introduces Maslow's hierarchy as an infrastructure-mediated behavioral predictor: when material security is threatened, higherorder political preferences contract, not from irrationality but from binding constraints on basic needs. Fifth, the closing circle-in which the fiscal architecture suppresses the fertility that would have generated the workers who would have paid the taxes to service the debt it created-is identified and quantified: CBO has revised its 2054 population projection downward by 10.8 million people, attributing the entire reduction to suppressed fertility. The demographic relief valve-immigrant-origin families reproducing above replacement while generating a net fiscal surplus of $14.5 trillion-is being shut by the same political coalition whose material interests it serves.

My findings indicate that the education and fertility benefits to undocumented students come with no significant unintended costs to other students. records.title: The evolution of civic capital in rural China: Sons and Voting in village elections
records.note: No abstract; sons and voting in Chinese village elections.
records.recovered_abstract: Patrilineal family norms shape household behavior in developing countries, yet their consequences for formal political participation have received little attention. Using data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) 2014, we estimate the effect of having a son on voting in village committee elections. OLS estimates with village fixed effects indicate that having at least one son raises turnout by 7.6 percentage points, an 18% increase relative to the sample mean. We instrument son status with the gender of the first child, plausibly exogenous under rural China&apos;s "one-and-a-half-child" policy. The 2SLS estimate of 7.7 percentage points closely mirrors the OLS baseline, indicating that selection from fertility behavior is limited. We identify two mechanisms. First, a local residence effect: patrilocal marriage norms keep sons, but not daughters, in the natal village, giving parents a stronger stake in local governance. Second, a face effect: having a son raises social standing within the village, raising the confidence to engage in public affairs. Both channels attenuate in urban areas where patriarchal norms are weaker. Kinship institutions thus shape who turns out in grassroots elections. By linking patrilineal norms to electoral turnout, we show that family-centered interests can complement rather than crowd out formal governance.

records.recovered_abstract: Marriage rates in China have declined markedly over the past decade, raising increasing concern among policymakers and scholars of family behavior. As part of the country’s broader pension reform, the New Rural Pension Scheme (NRPS) was introduced to improve old-age security for informal-sector workers. This study examines whether parental participation in the NRPS affects the marriage decisions of their adult children through intergenerational channels. Using three waves (2011, 2013, and 2015) of data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), I find that continuous participation of both parents in the NRPS increases the likelihood of children’s marriage by about 7–8 percentage points. The results are robust across alternative specifications and subsample analyses. Further evidence suggests that the NRPS promotes children’s marriage primarily by reinforcing the raising-children-for-old-age (RSOA) motive and by reducing parents’ caregiving needs. By highlighting the intergenerational spillover of social insurance on household formation, this study extends the literature on family responses to public pension programs and provides policy insights for addressing declining marriage and fertility rates in developing economies. records.title: Health Sharenting and a Child’s Right to Privacy
records.note: No abstract; sharenting and children's privacy.
records.recovered_abstract: The internet and social media represent a ubiquitous part of the American experience today. From birth, if not before, children are exposed to and influenced by social media. Parents turn to social media for parenting advice or to share stories about the parenting experience-fertility struggles, pregnancy, parenting children with disabilities or chronic or terminal illnesses, and much more. Some parents even make a living as parenting "influencers" or turn their children into "kidfluencers." All of this raises important questions. Should parents share intimate details about their children's lives? If so, should there be limits and how would such limits be enforced? The explosion of parents sharing information about their children's physical and mental health struggles online ("health sharenting") raises serious questions about consent and a child's right to privacy. Once this information is released into the public domain, there is no going back. It can be difficult, if not impossible, to erase information from the internet. For the rest of the child's life, others can find information about the child's physical or mental health. Raising awareness and creating space for parents to find support and advice is important, but at what cost? This Article queries whether the benefits of health sharenting outweigh the real and potential harms. It concludes by proposing a "presumption of privacy" in the parentchild relationship and how that presumption can be enforced.
